earlier_scan.source_named: Mead, David E. 1998. Proto-Bungku-Tolaki: reconstruction of its phonology and aspects of its morphosyntax (Rice PhD; contains Tomadino data); sulang.org unreachable
earlier_scan.note: Mead's Bungku-Tolaki materials plausibly state penultimate stress for Tomadino

new_statements.quote: All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages are open syllable languages, with the only syllable patterns being V and CV. Most roots are disyllabic, though occasionally three and four syllable roots are found. Stress is penultimate (non-phonemic), with suffixation usually precipitating stress movement. [p.16] ... I assume that in Proto-Bungku-Tolaki stress fell on the penultimate syllable, there being no reason to reconstruct otherwise. All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages also exhibit penultimate stress. [p.97] ... (g) In the absence of any stress marking, one can assume penultimate stress occurring on the next to last written vowel. [Mead 1999:101]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the page renders in and the scanned/text layers. Mead 1998 p.16 (scanned raha1237/scanned/), sec. 1.5 'Present-day sound systems': 'All present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages are open syllable languages, with the only syllable patterns being V and CV. Most roots are disyllabic, though occasionally three and four syllable roots are found. Stress is penultimate (non-phonemic), with suffixation usually precipitating stress movement.' -- verbatim as quoted; fn.4 on long vowels as two like vowels 'as may be argued from patterns of stress placement' also present. Mead 1998 p.97 (bung1269/ lines 344-348), end of sec. 3.1.2: 'I assume that in Proto-Bungku-Tolaki stress fell on the penultimate s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word (counted by written vowels, since all syllables are V or CV and there are no phonemic long vowels); stress is non-contrastive and shifts rightward under suffixation so as to stay penultimate in the suffixed word.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Tomadino. Suffixation 'usually' moves stress (Mead 1998:16). Phonetically long vowels are analysed as two like vowels and counted as such for stress (Mead 1998:16 fn.4; Mead 1999:102 (d)); a pre-stress lengthened vowel may reflect an intermediate pronunciation between VV and V (Mead 1999:102).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, on roots and suffixed words; the 1999 convention applies to citation-form wordlist items (Tomadino list 60, Sakita village, elicited by Mead 11 Jan 1989). The statement is made for 'all present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages' collectively, not for Tomadino alone; Mead is the only linguist to have recorded Tomadino data.
new_statements.identity_note: toma1248 is a language-level glottocode with no dialects (Mead 1999:63). The quoted statement is a family-wide generalisation ('all present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages') by the only linguist who has collected Tomadino data (Sakita village, 1989); no Tomadino-specific phonology exists (Mead 1999:103 lists phonologies only for Tolaki, Padoe, Mori, Moronene). The same Mead 1998 sentence has already been used for the sibling entries tola1247 and bung1269/raha1237 in this audit.
